abidjan-lagos-corridor-road-works-deaths.place: Noé, Aboisso, Assouba, Samo and Port-Bouët, along the Grand-Bassam–Aboisso–Noé road, Côte d’Ivoire
abidjan-lagos-corridor-road-works-deaths.point: Noé, the border town opposite Elubo in Ghana, where the project built the market platform the displaced traders were moved to (village point from OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second Phase Project of the Abidjan-Lagos Trade and Transport Facilitation Program (P116323), IDA grant H7870 of SDR 57.9 million (US$90 million equivalent) to the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire; Board approval 31 May 2012, actual closing 29 March 2019 (completion report ICR00004935, 18 December 2019; evaluation review ICRR0021995, 5 June 2020). The Bank partly suspended disbursements on Component B from December 2016 after safety and resettlement failures. The completion report rates the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory (ICR00004935, paragraph 47); the Independent Evaluation Group also rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory (ICRR0021995).

companies.name: Projet de Facilitation du Commerce et du Transport sur le Corridor Abidjan-Lagos (PFCTCAL) Project Implementation Unit
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report. It sat under the Ministry of Economy and Finance until December 2016, when it was reassigned to the Ministry of Economic Infrastructure as a condition of lifting the suspension; project management passed to the unit of the IDA-financed PRICI project on 30 November 2016. The completion report names no construction contractor.

companies.name: Ghana Highway Authority
companies.role: Road agency of Ghana’s Ministry of Roads and Highways, through its Road Safety and Environment Division; wrote the abbreviated resettlement plan for the 640 m dual carriageway and Noé bridge on the Ghanaian side, disclosed under the same project number in December 2017

abidjan-lagos-corridor-road-works-deaths.community: The completion report records 2,411 people affected by the works of Component B. Of those, 2,256 were compensated, which it puts at 94 per cent, and 155 could not be reached. FCFA 3.6 billion (US$7.2 million) was spent on the resettlement plan, of which FCFA 3.5 billion, 98 per cent, went directly to affected people and FCFA 56 million was placed in an escrow account. The affected people were at Port-Bouët, Samo, Assouba, Aboisso and Noé. The report says counterpart money had been set aside at appraisal so that everyone would be paid before civil works started, “however compensations were carried out with delays”, and that civil works went ahead while the resettlement plan had not been fully carried out four years into the project. At Noé the project built a platform of 8,800 square metres to move the affected traders onto; a Noé Traders Management Committee set up by Ministerial Order in June 2019 runs the new market. The borrower’s own report, printed in the completion report, says the resettlement of Noé’s traders after compensation “preserves the activities of the people affected by the project”, and that the works at the Noé parking lot were provisionally finished but had defects. On the Ghanaian side of the same crossing, the abbreviated resettlement plan of December 2017 sets a cut-off date of 19 October 2015 and counts 38 “total affected household heads/PAPs who will be losing structures and crops”, with compensation valued at GH¢389,513.95 (US$88,525.90). Payment is the responsibility of the Government of Ghana: the plan says the Ministry of Finance had already released the funds to the Ghana Highway Authority, pending the Bank’s approval of the plan. Two years after the cut-off date the plan records that “the PAPs have already stopped farming after the notification of the cut-off date”, that “continuous consultations have been going on to update the PAPs on the delay in the implementation of the RAP”, and that site visits on 27 to 29 November and 5 December 2017 found no new cocoa trees or other crops planted and nothing changed on the ground since the cut-off date, although planting around the houses had continued by agreement with the affected people until they were paid.
abidjan-lagos-corridor-road-works-deaths.killed_note: Five deaths are recorded on the road works and are left uncounted here because no document ties any one of them to the works. The completion report says Component B “was suspended between December 2016 and June 2017 because of serious occupational safety and road safety issues on the road works that resulted in 22 accidents, including five fatalities in 6 months” (ICR00004935, paragraph 62). The same report’s safeguards section says instead that there were “at least 22 accidents, including five fatalities, that had not been properly reported to the World Bank, and some of which had led to protests from local communities” (paragraph 71), which makes the count a floor. The report gives no cause for any individual death, does not say which of the dead were workers and which were road users, names nobody, and does not say which road section the accidents were on. Of the Component B road works, a footnote to the report records that IDA financed only the Aboisso–Noé section, about 59.2 km, the Grand-Bassam–Aboisso works being among those financed by the government’s counterpart funds, so the document does not establish which credit paid for the works where the deaths happened. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats the figure of at least 22 accidents including five fatalities, citing the report.
abidjan-lagos-corridor-road-works-deaths.outcome: The suspension was lifted after a nine-point action plan that moved project management to a new unit, added an environmental and a social specialist, and ordered safeguards, technical and safety audits. The road condition was improved on 113.59 km against a target of 130.3 km. The completion report says the overall safeguards were rated Moderately Unsatisfactory “during a significant period of implementation”, and that some of the accidents had led to protests from local communities.

abidjan-lagos-corridor-road-works-deaths.confidence_note: The deaths, the accident count, the number of people affected and the payment delays all come from the Bank’s own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group’s review of that report. No independent press report, court record or audit of the five deaths was found. The completion report says the five deaths followed safety failures on the works but gives no cause for any individual death and does not separate worker deaths from road-user deaths. Three different lengths are given for the suspension and are left as they stand: the completion report says seven months in its efficiency and implementation sections, says Component B was suspended between December 2016 and June 2017 in paragraph 62, and says in paragraph 77 that the team worked with the client for almost eight months to lift it, while the borrower’s own report printed in the same document gives “the long suspension of disbursements (8 months)” and the Independent Evaluation Group’s review says the suspension was lifted after eight months. The review attributes its account of the Noé platform and of physical cultural resources to “information provided by the team” rather than to a document, so neither is used here. The compensation figures for the Ghanaian side are the plan’s; no outcome document for the Ghanaian works was found.
abidjan-lagos-corridor-road-works-deaths.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 692 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The same figure is the total of the October 2011 resettlement plan’s census table, which counts 692 people recorded along the route and at the Vridi freight station, of whom 13 are households and 677 are managers of commercial, artisanal and service activities; the same plan says the census “identified a total of 695 people who will have to vacate the works right of way”. No outcome document counts anyone relocated.

lenders.role: Kribi Gas Power Project (P110177), IDA partial risk guarantee G-2090 of up to CFA 40 billion (US$82 million equivalent) to Kribi Power Development Company, backing the loans of local commercial lenders; Board approval 11 November 2011, effective 23 August 2012, closed in 2013 against an original closing of 2016 (completion report No. 136765-CM, 23 October 2019). The project was Environmental Category A and triggered the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources, indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement. The completion report rates the overall project outcome Satisfactory (paragraph 46). No Independent Evaluation Group review of this report was reachable.

lenders.role: Facility Agent for the lenders; the completion report says it led supervision of plant construction and of compliance with the Bank’s environmental and social safeguards, through an independent owner’s engineer

companies.name: Kribi Power Development Company (KPDC)
companies.role: Independent power producer created in 2008 to build and run the plant; the project’s implementing agency and borrower under the guaranteed loans

companies.name: Wartsila
companies.role: Named in the completion report as the only bidder to propose a detailed binding offer for the larger plant and as offering the lowest cost of generated electricity; the report says the choice of gas engines for the plant was made on the basis of that offer. It does not record who supplied the engines.

companies.name: Siemens France
companies.role: With KEC India, the preferred bidder for the engineering, procurement and construction contract on the 225 kV transmission line and the 11/225 kV substation

companies.name: KEC India
companies.role: Consortium partner with Siemens France on the transmission line and substation contract, as named in the completion report

companies.name: Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures (SNH)
companies.role: Cameroon’s state hydrocarbons company and sponsor of the Sanaga South gas pipeline that fuels the plant; through its Comité de Pilotage et de Suivi des Pipelines it assessed and paid the compensation for the Bipaga access road

kribi-gas-plant-land-and-crops-taken-mpo.community: The completion report says the 2012 annual monitoring report recorded the physical resettlement of 23 families, compensation for crops destroyed outside the transmission line corridor, and the restoration of polluted water courses. The completion report puts the onshore gas pipeline inside the project as an associated facility, within the scope of the environmental and social impact assessment updated in 2010. For the access road from the Edéa–Kribi national road to the SNH site at Bipaga, built for SNH’s own Sanaga-Sud pipeline project, a compensation note disclosed under the Bank project in March 2012 records payments actually made: 24 people were compensated for crops in the right of way, on the basis of expert valuation sheets listing the crops, the number of plants and the amount; three private properties with land titles were partly taken, of 5,543 square metres (FCFA 27,715,000), 846 square metres (FCFA 8,460,000) and 1,360 square metres (FCFA 6,800,000); and houses lost were paid for at market economic value, with the buildings described as mostly built of temporary materials. The payments were made on 23 September 2010 and 3 December 2010, a year before the Bank’s Board approved the guarantee, out of SNH’s own budget under Prime Ministerial Decree 2010/2341/PM of 3 August 2010, some by cheque and some in cash. SNH says the payments were peaceful and on time and that no dispute was recorded, and that the people living around the access road carried on farming, fishing and working in Kribi. Once the plant was running, low-frequency noise from the engines disturbed the villages around it. Measured noise was slightly above World Health Organization and IFC levels, but so were the baseline levels taken before the plant ran, which the report puts down to the site and the nearby highways. Local communities complained of vibration in their homes. KPDC insulated the roofs of affected homes with noise-suppression material and built a noise barrier wall near the turbines. The project also had an Indigenous Peoples Plan covering Bakola communities along the transmission line; on this the completion report records only that KPDC worked with the NGO Cameroon Ecology to help carry the plan out, and gives no outcome for those communities.
kribi-gas-plant-land-and-crops-taken-mpo.killed_note: The completion report records no deaths. It says no water pollution was recorded by the construction contractor and that no lost-time accidents were recorded after operations began in 2013. It gives no safety record for the construction period.
kribi-gas-plant-land-and-crops-taken-mpo.displaced_label: 23 families physically resettled, from the project’s 2012 annual monitoring report as quoted in the Bank’s completion report
kribi-gas-plant-land-and-crops-taken-mpo.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 680 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report gives no other count of people relocated, and does not say where the 23 families went.
kribi-gas-plant-land-and-crops-taken-mpo.outcome: The 216 MW plant was built and the completion report rates the project Satisfactory. The report also records that electricity supply from KPDC depends on the government paying a tariff compensation to the distributor ENEO to cover the gap between its costs and regulated tariffs, and that payments were irregular.

The land and crop payments at Bipaga are documented in detail, with amounts and dates, but the document was written by SNH, the company that made the payments and that ran the pipeline project the access road was built for, and it names no dispute. Those payments were made in September and December 2010, before the Bank’s Board approved the guarantee on 11 November 2011; the completion report brings the pipeline inside the project as an associated facility. No independent press report, court record or audit of either was found.

pdue-cameroon-unpaid-compensation-yaound.title: Compensation still unpaid months after closing in Cameroon’s urban upgrading project
pdue-cameroon-unpaid-compensation-yaound.place: Yaoundé, with works also in Douala, Bamenda, Maroua and Mbalmayo, Cameroon
pdue-cameroon-unpaid-compensation-yaound.point: Yaoundé, the city where the completion report says two compensation payments were still waiting for presidential clearance (city point from OpenStreetMap); the project’s Phase 2 resettlement plans cover the Kondengui and Ekounou quarters of Yaoundé 4 and the Efoulan and Nsimeyong quarters

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urban and Water Development Support Project, known as PDUE (P084002), IDA credit 4313-CM of SDR 53.3 million (US$80 million equivalent) and an additional financing, credit 4820-CM, of SDR 18.9 million (US$28.7 million equivalent) from Pilot Crisis Response Window resources; Board approval 29 May 2007, actual closing 31 August 2015 (completion report ICR00003619, 29 February 2016; evaluation review ICRR0020199, 28 June 2016). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Both documents rate the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the risk to development outcome High.

companies.name: Project Coordination Unit, Ministry of Housing and Urban Development (MINHDU)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the urban components, a unit kept inside MINHDU after closing; it paid compensation directly or through the municipalities. The completion report names no construction contractor.

pdue-cameroon-unpaid-compensation-yaound.community: The completion report says counterpart money was secured so that the project unit, directly or through the municipalities, could pay compensation to the 585 people affected by the project. Of those, 88 per cent had been compensated as of 31 January 2016, against 51 per cent at the closing date of 31 August 2015, for CFAF 401 million, which the report puts at 88 per cent of the amount due. The report says payments had markedly progressed since the closing date “but two for Yaoundé were still awaiting the presidential clearance at the time of this report”. The Bank’s involuntary resettlement policy was rated only partly complied with, Moderately Unsatisfactory in early 2014 and again at closing. The report says the delays were beyond the project’s control: the national rules for taking land and paying for it ran through several administrative steps, including a Presidential Decree clearing the list of affected people that could take months to come out, and further decrees were needed to add people left out of the first assessments. Phase 2 resettlement plans were approved only at the end of 2014. For Phase 1 the report says no standalone resettlement plans had been prepared where works cut across parts of urban plots, while adding that “in practice though, as noted in supervision reports, the PCU had complied with the policy’s requirements through consultations on the project’ benefits”. It says that in many cases owners agreed to hand land over to the public domain with no money paid, which saved time on the works, and that other families were paid for damage. For Phase 2 the rule was tightened so that works could not start before people were paid. The report says full payment of the outstanding compensation “remains of utmost importance”, and that the Bank made fully resolving the compensation legacy a condition of approving a follow-on operation.
pdue-cameroon-unpaid-compensation-yaound.killed_note: Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group’s review records a death or an injury on this project.
pdue-cameroon-unpaid-compensation-yaound.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 536 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 585 people affected and gives no count of anyone relocated.
pdue-cameroon-unpaid-compensation-yaound.outcome: Payments had moved on since the closing date but were not finished when the completion report was written in February 2016, with two for Yaoundé awaiting presidential clearance. The Bank attached the condition that the compensation legacy be fully resolved before the follow-on “Inclusive Cities” operation went to its Board.

abidjan-riviera-2-shop-workers-unpaid-wa.point: Riviéra 2, Cocody, Abidjan, the site of the underpass where the ten shop employees worked (neighbourhood point from OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Emergency Urban Infrastructure Project (P110020), IDA grant H397-CI of SDR 57.10 million (US$94 million equivalent) and an additional grant H591-CI of SDR 33.10 million (US$50 million equivalent), of which SDR 9.93 million (US$15 million equivalent) came from Pilot Crisis Response Window resources; Board approval 12 June 2008, closing 31 March 2014 against an original date of 15 September 2012 (completion report ICR00003208, 29 January 2015; evaluation review ICRR14735, 20 April 2015). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. The completion report rates the overall outcome Highly Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rates it Satisfactory, finding minor shortcomings.

companies.name: Mission d’Appui à la Conduite d’Opérations Municipales (MACOM)
companies.role: Chosen as the project’s implementing and coordinating agency because its procurement and accounting staff already knew Bank procedures; the project coordination unit under it recruited a safeguards expert and a social expert in January 2009, who worked with the Agence Nationale de l’Environnement. The completion report names no construction contractor.

abidjan-riviera-2-shop-workers-unpaid-wa.community: Resettlement plans were prepared for four sites in Abidjan: the footbridge at Williamsville, the underpass at Riviera 2, the road at M’Badon, and the bridge and connecting road over the ravine in Cocody. The borrower’s report, printed as an annex to the completion report, says unforeseen impacts on local residents occurred during the rehabilitation of the M’Badon road, where access to shops was restricted, and during the construction of the Cocody zone 7-9 bridge, where third parties were damaged when a site access road was opened. For those cases it says the coordination unit “has ensured that Project-Affected Persons (PAPs) were duly compensated”, and that “a total of 629 PAPs have been compensated to the amount of FCFA 857,568,478 for a total of 639 PAPs identified. It remains to reimburse the salaries of 10 store employees affected by the Riviera 2 constructions due to technical unemployment, for whom salaries were pre-financed by employers, who have however failed to produce documentary evidence of this pre-financing to justify their refund.” On the annex’s account the ten were paid their wages by their employers; what remained unpaid was the project’s reimbursement of those wages. The same annex says an environmental and social review mission recruited in 2012 confirmed compliance with the project’s safeguard instruments. The main text of the same completion report says instead that the plans “provided compensation to all 639 persons affected by temporary closures causing loss of income due to works at these sites”, and that no other safeguard action was needed and the safeguards rating was satisfactory throughout.
abidjan-riviera-2-shop-workers-unpaid-wa.killed_note: Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group’s review records a death or an injury on this project.
abidjan-riviera-2-shop-workers-unpaid-wa.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 519 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The documents count 639 people affected by temporary closures and loss of income, and no one relocated.
abidjan-riviera-2-shop-workers-unpaid-wa.outcome: The reimbursement of the ten store employees’ wages was still outstanding when the completion report was written in January 2015, the annex giving as the reason that the employers who had pre-financed those wages had not produced documentary evidence of it. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review repeats the completion report’s main text that all 639 affected people were compensated and does not mention the ten.

kimbanseke-inga-kinshasa-line-pending-co.drop_reason: Cut by the checker. Limb (b) is not met: the harm is a pending claim of unstated content, with no count, no sum, no date and no statement of what any claimant lost, and the sentence that carries it also records the opposite. The deciding sentence is in the Independent Evaluation Group’s review ICRR0021847, safeguards section: “The ICR provides little detail on the status of compliance with individual safeguard policies. However, it indicates that at project closing, all triggered safeguards were rated Moderately Satisfactory, but there were several pending social and safeguard issues relating to dam safety, the arrangements to get rid of hazardous materials linked to the control of the black fly nuisance, and claims from Kimbanseke project-affected persons (PAPs). SNEL did confirm that the rehabilitation of the people affected by the construction of the second Inga-Kinshasa T-Line was completed, and there was agreement with stakeholders on how to close the process (the line would not be put into operation until the payment process was concluded).” Kimbanseke is a commune of Kinshasa of over a million people, not a site, so this is thinner than bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears, which is the standing edge for limb (b) and names a site and a count of cases. The project’s own completion report is not reachable on any route tried and the review is the only account of it. Other outcome material checked and found not to carry the case: the appraisal document’s 270 and 129 households are what the project expected to affect; the April 2011 draft resettlement plan for the project (RP1135 v2, the PMEDE involuntary resettlement plan) records in the past tense that 229 families were censused at the affected sites, 211 of them in Kinshasa with the largest number in Kimbanseke commune, that the amounts were negotiated and agreements on them formalised, and that 43 resident owners, 137 non-resident owners and 49 tenants or rent-free occupants were counted, but every loss in it carries a future verb — 141 houses and 1,537 fruit trees “will” be destroyed, US$2,315,477 of compensation is “provided for”, and the plan’s execution is given as a nine-month programme still to run. Joining that 2011 census to the 2018 pending claims would be the checker’s inference: neither document refers to the other. The review’s own data sheet material is kept in the log, including that the borrower contribution of US$38.0 million ended up nil and that the review records a disagreement inside the completion report, whose data sheet rates outcome Moderately Satisfactory while its main text rates it Moderately Unsatisfactory. ICIJ gives 266 for this project.
kimbanseke-inga-kinshasa-line-pending-co.checker_note: The writer named this entry the weakest in the batch and wrote that a checker who cut it would not be wrong to. The source list also carried the resettlement plan under the title “Plan de réinstallation du MEADE”; the document’s own cover reads PMEDE, and it is this project’s plan, not another project’s.

dropped_card.community: At the time the project closed on 30 June 2018, the Independent Evaluation Group’s review says all triggered safeguard policies were rated Moderately Satisfactory, but that several social and safeguard issues were still open, among them “claims from Kimbanseke project-affected persons”. The review adds that SNEL confirmed the rehabilitation of the people affected by the building of the second Inga–Kinshasa transmission line was complete, that there was agreement with stakeholders on how to close the process, and that the line would not be switched on until the payment process was finished. At appraisal the project was not expected to involve taking land or resettlement for the rehabilitation of Inga 1 and 2, but about 270 households were expected to be affected by land acquisition for the transmission line and about 129 households by the distribution works; resettlement plans were prepared for those anticipated resettlements. The review says the completion report gives little detail on compliance with the individual safeguard policies.
dropped_card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 266 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The 270 and 129 households in the appraisal document are what the project expected to affect, not a count of anyone relocated; no document reachable here counts people actually moved.
dropped_card.outcome: The compensation process at Kimbanseke was unfinished when the project closed, with the second Inga–Kinshasa line held out of service until payments were concluded. A Bank review of financial management of this project and of the Southern Africa Power Market Project found that SNEL had systematically failed to apply the recommendations of external auditors and Bank supervision teams, that several ineligible expenditures had been identified, and that financial management of both operations was unsatisfactory.

kinshasa-water-works-land-and-houses-tak.community: The water component extended the distribution network into poor quarters in the south and south-west of Kinshasa, in the communes of Mont Ngafula, Ngaliema, Lemba and Selembao, and built two reservoirs on the Mont Kimwenza Sebo and Kimbondo hills, a pumping station, and a catchment plant on the Lukaya river. Every count of the people is the June 2010 resettlement plan’s, written before the works began. It counts 72 households affected and 245 people in them: 41 at the first reservoir site, 7 at the pumping station, 5 at the second reservoir and 19 at the Lukaya site. Of the 72, it counts 30 losing land or structures, 23 losing their housing and 19 losing crops. It records the destruction across the three hill sites of various buildings, small houses, fences and foundations, and at the Lukaya site 72 fruit trees and 3 food gardens of cassava, and a permanent loss of 9,306 square metres of cultivable land, which it gives as 517 market-garden beds. The completion report says the start of works was put off from November 2009, when the contract was awarded, to January 2011, over who should pay the compensation and clear the sites. Cash indemnities of US$1,215,322 were then paid to the people affected by the water component. A non-governmental organisation was hired to help them put the money into income-generating work; 72 heads of household were trained in how to use their compensation that way, which the report says benefited 245 people in the affected households. The completion report concludes that all works were carried out in full respect of the safeguards instruments and that the Bank’s environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement policies were fully complied with, while noting that the frameworks themselves were prepared 13 months after the project became effective, against the six months the financing agreement allowed, and that the Bank’s team and management “ensured that no construction works took place prior to the completion and disclosure of the safeguards instruments”.
kinshasa-water-works-land-and-houses-tak.killed_note: Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group’s review records a death or an injury on this project.
kinshasa-water-works-land-and-houses-tak.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 245 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The 72 households, the 245 people and the breakdown of 30 losing land or structures, 23 losing their housing and 19 losing crops are all figures from the June 2010 resettlement plan, written before the works started in January 2011, not counts from an outcome document. The completion report carries the same two figures but attaches them to something else: it says 72 heads of household were trained in how to use their compensation for income-generating activities, “benefiting 245 people in the affected households”. No document reachable here says how many people were actually moved or where they went.
kinshasa-water-works-land-and-houses-tak.outcome: The compensation was paid and the works went ahead from January 2011. The completion report records no unpaid balance and no dispute over the payments.

takon-landfill-land-taken-porto-novo.community: The completion report says the government had to spend money it had set aside for its own share of the project on “unforeseen social measures that needed to be taken during the resettlement of communities living near the Takon landfill”. Those measures were three classroom blocks, eight toilets, roads, clinics, a community centre, electricity and a small-scale water supply, amounting to CFA 830 million, and the report says they were supplied to compensate communities whose land was taken to build the landfill at Takon, near Porto-Novo. Because that money went on the compensation, the government could not meet its 10 per cent share of the original credit or its 15 per cent share of the additional financing, and in July 2011 asked for funds to be reallocated. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review gives the same account and adds that the landfill was not operating when the project closed: delays at the National Board for Procurement Control meant the operator’s contract was not signed until six months after the closing date. A footnote in the completion report records that resettlement was not planned during the programme’s first phase, but “some resettlement activity took place without a resettlement framework being in place”. Both documents say the project complied with all safeguard requirements, that resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out before civil works began, and that the Benin Environment Agency certified the works; the completion report rates safeguards satisfactory.

takon-landfill-land-taken-porto-novo.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 243 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. Neither Bank document counts the households or people whose land was taken at Takon, or anyone relocated.
takon-landfill-land-taken-porto-novo.outcome: The communities received the buildings and services rather than cash. The landfill they gave up land for was still not being exploited at project closure, the operator’s contract being signed six months after the closing date; the Independent Evaluation Group’s review says the landfill was “still not fully functional by project closure”.

drc-urban-project-injury-threats-and-wor.community: The completion report counts 1,078 people affected by the project, identified through resettlement plans, of whom 1,041 were compensated for a total of US$155,918. The report says the rest did not present themselves to receive compensation, that the secretariat and local authorities tried to locate and contact them in each case, and that US$18,984 has been reserved with the local governments should those efforts succeed; it does not print a figure for how many people that is. Seventy-nine occupational health and safety incidents were recorded. Seventy-five were minor, three were serious and one, a fall from height causing serious injury, was treated as severe and reported to Bank management through its incident response procedure; the report says root causes were analysed, corrective measures developed, and the secretariat supplied documentation of the injured person’s treatment and full recovery. Three cases of non-compliance were documented. Two were works starting before the resettlement plan had been carried out, one of them before the contract had even been signed; in one of those the Bank told the government the investment would not be eligible for project money and no project funds were used, which a footnote gives as the reason no infrastructure was financed by the project in Goma, and in the other the resettlement plan was updated and the works allowed to continue. In Kolwezi, a project mission in February 2019 found 13 people losing income on Avenue Gazumbu — among them a hairdresser, a phone-kiosk operator and a pharmacy seller, listed by name, with GPS points, and assessed at US$1,195 in all, of which US$150 was assistance to people counted as vulnerable — whom an earlier consultant had missed: the 2016 study reported finding no affected people on that avenue, so no resettlement plan was written, no cut-off date was published and no signs were put up to stop new occupation of the right of way. The mayor’s office said it was ready to pay the 13 so they would clear the route before works began. At Kananga, the project’s own report on carrying out the resettlement plan for the erosion-control works at the MONUSCO site records that on 16 June 2021 one household head, counted as 15 affected persons, was paid US$5,650, all of what the plan provided: US$4,000 for the house and US$1,600 for fruit trees and family crops, with US$50 for one person assessed as vulnerable. Kananga city hall put up US$4,000 of that and the project US$1,650, in a table the report heads as funds for paying affected people who had been left out. The report says the household, that of Laurent Nkashama, moved into a house bought on the spot before the old one was pulled down, that the operation passed without incident, and that a grievance committee opened its registers at the town hall and in Mulombodi quarter on 19 June 2021.
drc-urban-project-injury-threats-and-wor.suppression: The completion report records that a person who had told the Bank of a possible failure of compliance on a construction site in Mbandaka “was allegedly subsequently threatened by provincial authorities”. The Bank sent a field mission at once, which it says confirmed both that the site complied and that the complainant was safe; a safeguards compliance audit followed and found no other case of non-compliance, and the Bank says it kept in regular touch with the complainant. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review records the same episode, without the word allegedly, as “a complainant reported being threatened by the provincial authorities after reporting a potential lack of compliance on a construction site in Mbandaka”. The review also divides the three cases of non-compliance differently from the completion report, counting works started before the contract was signed and works started before the resettlement plan was carried out as two separate cases.
drc-urban-project-injury-threats-and-wor.killed_note: Neither document records a death. The severe safety incident was a fall from height; the completion report says the injured person was treated and fully recovered.
drc-urban-project-injury-threats-and-wor.displaced_label: 15 people in one household resettled from Avenue Lithanie, Mulombodi quarter, Kananga, in the project’s own June 2021 report on carrying out the resettlement plan
drc-urban-project-injury-threats-and-wor.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 230 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The 15 is the only count of people actually resettled in any outcome document reachable here; the completion report’s 1,078 is a count of people affected across all the project cities.
drc-urban-project-injury-threats-and-wor.outcome: All the safety cases and the grievances were recorded as closed before the project ended. US$18,984 of compensation stayed unpaid, reserved with local governments for the affected people who never came forward. The completion report rates the project Moderately Unsatisfactory overall, and says Kananga still faces serious gully erosion threatening other infrastructure.

cote-divoire-urgent-electricity-rehabili.drop_reason: Neither limb of the forward rule is met. Outcome document checked: the completion report of 20 November 2015 (ICR3428), paragraph 68, the whole social safeguards paragraph. It says the involuntary resettlement policy was triggered, that of 89 subprojects for upgrading and expanding the distribution network under Component 1, 22 were found to require Resettlement Action Plans 'covering about 200 persons', that 'the resettlement aspect was related mainly to the impact on street vendors and artisans along the routes where the underground lines were replaced', and that the plans 'were successfully completed through regular supervision by the Bank and the PCU'. Compliance was rated satisfactory from 2009 to March 2011 and moderately satisfactory thereafter, the downgrade being attributed to the electoral crisis and then to delays in selecting a consulting firm to prepare the plans and hiring an extra expert. liberia-emergency-infrastructure-dropped.drop_reason: Neither limb of the forward rule is met. Outcome document checked: the completion report of 26 June 2013 (ICR2630), paragraph 37, the whole safeguards paragraph, plus the solid waste outcome section at paragraph 54 and the borrower performance section at paragraph 84. Paragraph 37 records the one failing: 'During implementation a case of non-compliance with OP 4.12 was recorded for sanitation works at locations along the Metsurado River where solid waste cleanup was to be done. Works were stopped and deferred until the RAP was prepared.' The works were halted before anyone was moved, and the same paragraph concludes 'it is considered that overall safeguard compliance was satisfactory'; paragraph 84 adds that 'funding for resettlement was made available in a timely manner'. The outcome section records the volume of waste removed, 19 public toilets rehabilitated and the Whein Town landfill financed to about 80 per cent of works, and gives no count of anyone relocated and no compensation shortfall. The project's own resettlement plan of July 2008 identifies 99 households in the area to be cleared of refuse 'who will be displaced', a figure in a draft plan that no outcome document picks up. No evaluation review was reachable for this project. Independent reporting on the Whein Town landfill (FrontPage Africa, 29 September 2026) records residents' accounts of foul-smelling water, mosquitoes, rodents and malaria, with no test results, no illness counts and no compensation, and attributes the 2011 landfill to the Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation project rather than to this credit, so it cannot be tied to this financing. ICIJ gives 431 for this project. Checked and added by the checker: paragraph 43 of the same report says “the solid waste activities were curtailed after they exceeded the intermediate outcome and have been continued under the Bank funded EMUS Project”, which is why no harm at the Whein Town landfill attaches to this credit. The Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation project (P115664) is the credit the press account points to and is a separate row.

nigeria-ramp-2-dropped.drop_reason: Dropped because the whole of it would be a count of people affected plus a compensation delay whose stated consequence is delay to the project, which the forward rule excludes. Outcome documents checked: the completion report of 21 June 2021, paragraphs 48 to 61, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 2 December 2021, its safeguards section. The completion report's paragraph 57 says 'Adamawa, Enugu, and Osun states experienced delays in implementing Resettlement Action Plans (RAPs, with 2,423 affected persons compensated for a total amount of Naira123,528,553) occasioned by late release of counterpart funds by State Governments' — that is, all 2,423 were paid. Paragraph 49 adds that Enugu's unit received no funds in 2014 and 'were not able to cover operating expenses and payment of compensation under the Resettlement Action Plans', with total outstanding counterpart funding of Naira 3,591,869,010 at the October 2016 mid-term review. The review states the consequence the completion report does not: the delayed compensation 'slowed down project implementation and was one of the reasons for the project closing date extension'. There is no count of anyone relocated, no unpaid balance and no recorded loss to any identifiable person. The grievance mechanism logged 123 complaints, all addressed. The only other safeguards finding, that shrines were encountered along priority roads in Enugu State in June 2016 and the matter solved by revising an abbreviated resettlement plan, exists in the review solely as what 'the project team subsequently informed IEG', with the revised plan noted as 'not archived in WB docs'. Two kidnappings of contractor staff in Osun and Niger states between February and April 2019 are recorded; they are harm to the contractor's employees by third parties, not harm caused by the project. The 2015, 2016 and 2019 resettlement plans and addenda in the cache are all plans. ICIJ gives 428 for this project.
